title: ECB raises interest rates to 2.5% on September 10, warns Middle East conflict will keep inflation elevated into 2027
dek: The European Central Bank raised its main interest rate to 2.5% on Thursday, September 10, citing Middle East conflict as a driver of elevated energy prices and persistent inflation. ECB President Christine Lagarde stated inflation will remain high longer than anticipated, with headline inflation not expected to return to target until the first half of 2027.
author: The GoCheckMyNews Desk
key_fact: The ECB's rate increase to 2.5%, its highest since March 2025, comes as Brent crude passed $105 per barrel and EU gas storage sits at 67%, well below the five-year average of 84%.
bottom_line: ECB officials will announce any further rate decisions at their next monetary policy meeting; markets are pricing in a path of sustained elevation in borrowing costs through at least mid-2027, contingent on Middle East energy markets remaining disrupted. If the Strait of Hormuz were to reopen or a military de-escalation were to occur, inflation expectations and rate paths could shift sharply downward.
body: The European Central Bank raised its main interest rate to 2.5% on Thursday, September 10, its highest level since March 2025, as energy prices surge on military escalation between the United States and Iran. ECB President Christine Lagarde stated the bank believes "inflation will be longer lasting than we had anticipated," signaling that elevated borrowing costs will persist across the eurozone longer than previously expected.

The rate increase reflects a shift in the ECB's inflation outlook driven by soaring energy prices. According to the Guardian's reporting, Brent crude passed $105 per barrel before slipping back to about $104.50, a 3.3% rise on the day. British gas prices rose to above 203p per therm, the highest since December 2022, per the Guardian. Dutch wholesale gas, the EU standard, passed €80 per megawatt hour for the first time since January 2023, with front-month contracts trading 3.4% higher at €82.56 per megawatt hour, the Guardian reports.

The ECB lifted its forecast for eurozone economic growth in 2026 to 0.9%, up from 0.8% in June, according to the Guardian. Yet the bank now expects inflation to average 3% in 2026 and believes headline inflation will return to around target only towards the end of 2027, supported by higher interest rates. Lagarde noted that food inflation had remained low at 1.2% but is likely to increase in response to higher oil and gas prices.

Energy storage constraints intensify the inflation pressure. EU gas stores are only 67% full, well below the five-year average of 84%, per the Guardian's reporting. The Guardian reports that the latest US and Iran attacks on ships occurred in the Strait of Hormuz this week, and the BBC reports the war has led to the effective closure of the strait, preventing supplies of oil and gas from the Gulf from reaching global markets.

The rate increase pushed government bond yields to levels unseen in years. According to the Guardian, the interest rate on 10-year UK government bonds (gilts) hit 5.36%, the highest since August 2007. Germany's 30-year government bond yield rose 2.5 basis points to 5.08%, the highest since December 2003, and its 10-year yield hit 3.45%, the highest since April 2011, the Guardian reports. France's 10-year government bond yield reached 4.344%, the highest since October 2008 and up 1 basis point, according to the Guardian. The BBC reports that yields on UK 20- and 30-year bonds reached levels not seen since 1998.

Meanwhile, the US Treasury announced a response to the bond market sell-off. According to the Guardian, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the US would buy back $6 billion worth of government debt to alleviate the sell-off in the US bond market. Yet the Guardian reports that the yield on 10-year treasuries rose to a three-year high after the announcement, with bond buyers considering the package inadequate.
The UK price cap is already due to increase by 3.6% at the start of October, with the next change after that coming in January, per the BBC.
